name: Surveyor 3
transmission: May 4, 1967 — I sent my final signal to Earth. After several days exploring the lunar surface, I fell silent as the long lunar night began.
story: Surveyor 3 was a test lander: could the Moon hold up a spacecraft, or would it sink? On 20 April 1967 it touched down in Oceanus Procellarum, bounced twice, and settled safely. Over two weeks it sent 6,326 pictures and used a scoop to dig four trenches. Its soil tests showed the ground was firm enough for Apollo. In 1969 Apollo 12 astronauts landed about 180 metres away and brought its camera home.

name: Apollo 11 descent stage
status: Still at Tranquility Base, left behind on July 21, 1969
transmission: July 21, 1969 — The Apollo 11 crew departed the lunar surface and left me behind. I was not designed to operate as an independent transmitting spacecraft, so I sent no further signals to Earth.
story: Eagle carried Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin down to the Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969. The descent stage was the lower half: its engine slowed the landing, and its legs held the lander steady. When the astronauts left, it stayed behind as the launch platform for the ascent stage. It is still there, along with the footprints and the experiments they set up.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
status: Still parked on the Moon since August 2, 1971
transmission: August 2, 1971 — The Apollo 15 astronauts completed their final lunar exploration activities with me, then left me on the Moon. I did not continue sending independent signals after the mission.
story: The first lunar car reached the Moon with Apollo 15 in 1971. Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin unfolded it from Falcon's cargo bay and drove it across the Hadley–Apennine site. The rover let them travel farther from the lander than ever before: three drives totalling 27.9 kilometres, returning 77 kilograms of rock and soil. It is still parked on the surface, its batteries dead and its wheels silent.

name: Apollo 17 ALSEP
status: Switched off from Earth on September 30, 1977
transmission: September 30, 1977 — NASA switched me off from Earth. After nearly five years collecting information about moonquakes, temperature, and the lunar environment, my scientific data transmissions came to an end.
story: Apollo 17 left five experiments grouped around a central station in the Taurus–Littrow valley. Powered by a small plutonium generator, the ALSEP measured heat escaping the Moon, tiny moonquakes, the thin lunar atmosphere, and specks of cosmic dust striking the surface. The instruments ran for almost five years, long after the astronauts went home, and were switched off on 30 September 1977 to save money. They are still sitting there.

name: Viking 1 lander
status: Operations stopped after a faulty command on November 11, 1982
transmission: November 11, 1982 — I sent my final communications after more than six years on Mars. A faulty command interrupted my contact with Earth, and all attempts to restore communication were unsuccessful.
story: Viking 1 became the first spacecraft to land successfully on Mars on 20 July 1976, on the slopes of Chryse Planitia. It sent the first pictures from the surface, measured temperatures from −123°F before dawn to −27°F in the afternoon, and used a robotic arm to sample the soil. Its biology lab found no organic molecules but plenty of sulfur. A bad command from Earth in 1982 ended contact.

name: Sojourner
transmission: September 27, 1997 — At 10:23 UTC, NASA received my final data transmission. I had explored Mars for 83 days, far exceeding my original seven-day mission plan.
story: Pathfinder bounced to a stop in Ares Vallis on 4 July 1997, inside airbags, and opened to release a microwave-oven-sized rover named Sojourner. It was the first rover on Mars. Over 12 weeks it studied rocks and soil, sent 550 images, and helped show that ancient Mars had a warmer, wetter past. Its last data reached Earth on 27 September 1997, when the lander's battery gave out.

name: Opportunity
status: Silent since June 10, 2018 after driving 45.16 km
transmission: June 10, 2018 — I sent my final data to Earth during a massive Martian dust storm. My last message was an incomplete image of the darkened sky, ending my 14-year exploration.
story: Opportunity landed in Meridiani Planum on 24 January 2004 for a 90-day mission. It kept going for 14 years, driving 45.16 kilometres and finding minerals that form in water, such as hematite and clays. Those discoveries helped prove ancient Mars once had liquid water. In 2018 a planet-wide dust storm blocked the Sun and covered its solar panels. Its last signal reached Earth on 10 June 2018.

name: Ingenuity
transmission: November 26, 2024 — I last successfully communicated with Perseverance. After rotor-blade damage ended my flying, I remained on Mars while the rover relayed my communications.
story: Mars's air is about one percent as thick as Earth's, so flying there is hard. Ingenuity arrived under Perseverance in 2021 and became the first aircraft to fly under control on another planet. Its first hop on 19 April 2021 was meant to be one of only five. Instead it flew 72 times over nearly three years, scouting ahead for the rover and climbing to 24 metres. A damaged rotor blade ended its flying in January 2024.

name: Pioneer 10
status: January 23, 2003: Pioneer 10's last signal is received on Earth
transmission: January 23, 2003 — Earth received my final faint signal from billions of miles away. My last complete scientific telemetry had arrived earlier, on April 27, 2002, as my power supply gradually weakened.
story: Pioneer 10 left Earth in 1972 and became the first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and fly past Jupiter, sending back the first close-up images of the giant planet in 1973. It then kept going, crossing Neptune's orbit in 1983 as the first human-made object to leave the planets behind. Its power faded slowly. The last signal arrived on 23 January 2003 from 7.6 billion miles away — nearly 11 hours in transit.

name: NEAR Shoemaker
status: February 12, 2001: NEAR touched down on Eros, the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid
transmission: February 28, 2001 — I made my final contact with Earth after successfully landing on asteroid Eros. Although I was not designed to survive as a lander, I continued collecting and transmitting valuable scientific information for about two weeks.
story: NEAR Shoemaker was sent to asteroid Eros. It arrived in 2000 as the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, mapping its cratered surface and measuring its gravity. When its mission ended, engineers tried something new: they gently guided it down. On 12 February 2001 it became the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid, then kept sending data for two weeks before the cold silenced it. It was renamed for geologist Eugene Shoemaker.

name: Kepler
status: October 30, 2018: Retired after completing its second mission; still orbits the Sun
transmission: November 15, 2018 — I received my final commands from Earth, officially ending my communications with mission control. After discovering thousands of planets beyond our solar system, I entered retirement.
story: Kepler stared at one patch of sky for years, watching for the tiny dips in starlight caused by planets passing in front of their stars. Launched in 2009, it found more than 2,600 planets, including rocky worlds and solar systems packed tightly around their suns. It showed that planets are common — perhaps more common than stars. When it ran out of fuel in 2018, it was retired, still orbiting the Sun.

name: Dawn
transmission: October 31, 2018 — I lost my radio signal after running out of hydrazine fuel, which helped me point my antenna toward Earth. I had completed an extraordinary journey exploring Vesta and Ceres.
story: Dawn visited two worlds in the asteroid belt: Vesta, a giant asteroid, and Ceres, a dwarf planet. Launched in 2007, it became the first spacecraft to orbit two different bodies beyond Earth. At Vesta it found a layered interior and gullies; at Ceres it found bright salt deposits and signs that briny water once rose from inside. When its fuel ran out in 2018, it stayed in orbit around Ceres.
